Tory alludes to New Orleans, Louisiana rappers, Birdman and Lil Wayne. The two rappers met when Wayne was just 8-years-old, and they formed a father/son like bond. Wayne signed to Birdman’s Cash Money Records in 1995 at the age of 12. During his tenure with Cash Money, Wayne collaborated with Birdman numerous times, including collaborative albums like October 2006’s Like Father, Like Son.

In December 2014, Wayne announced that he wanted to leave Cash Money for holding up the release of his Tha Carter V album. Wayne later sued the label for $51 dollars, starting a beef with his former mentor and father figure. In June 2018, Wayne was finally released from his contract.

Wayne and Birdman later reconciled in August 2018 at Lil Weezyana Fest in New Orleans where Birdman issued Wayne a public apology.

meaning:
50 is comparing the story told by Tory to those of  2Pac and Nas, both known for their controversial lyrics and songs about ghetto lives.

In particular, 50 refers to “Brenda’s Got a Baby”, the solo debut single by Tupac Shakur, and tenth track from his 1991 debut album, 2Pacalypse Now. The song, which features R&B singer Dave Hollister, is about a 12-year-old girl named Brenda who lives in a ghetto and has a baby she can’t support. The song explores the issue of teen pregnancy and its effect on young mothers and their families. Like many of Shakur’s songs, “Brenda’s Got a Baby” draws from the plight of the impoverished. Using Brenda to represent young mothers in general, Shakur criticises the low level of support from the baby’s father, the government, and society in general. Shakur wrote the song when he read a newspaper article about a 12-year-old girl who became pregnant from her cousin and threw the baby into a trash compactor.



50 also mentions Nas because they both sampled the beat from Sting’s “Shape of my Heart" off his 1993 LP, Ten Summoner’s Tales.

This line is deeper than might be immediately evident. Tory uses boxing terminology (left hooks and right jabs) as metaphorical wordplay, since a ‘hook’ can also refer to the chorus of a song and to ‘write a jab’ is to come up with a punchline.



It should also be noted that left hooks and right jabs are less common than right hooks and left jabs, since most fighters stand in the orthodox position, leading with their left limbs. This could imply that Tory Lanez takes a less predictable or traditional approach to his flow/fighting style.

He follows this series of references by mentioning that he doesn’t even write his music—rather, all of his lyrics are “off top” or improvised. This, too, is a double entendre, because telling the barber to take “everything off the top” is a way of asking for a bald cut—a look that Tory is known for rocking.
